verdict.rationale: Proa documents islands that emit server-rendered HTML plus per-island JavaScript, and incremental adoption paths: proxying one route to Proa while the rest stays on Next.js or Rails, and calling Proa over FFI from Node, Go, Python, Ruby, or Java. That suggests components can be rendered into existing backends, but the evidence never shows islands being embedded into an existing server-rendered page; adoption is documented per route, not per component. Missing for 10: explicit docs for mounting interactive islands inside an existing non-Proa HTML page, an FFI example rendering a hydrated component into a foreign template, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can drop the framework into an existing server-rendered HTML page and render interactive components without rewriting the whole page

citations.quote: Add signals and event handlers, and Proa emits the server-rendered HTML plus the JavaScript required for that island
Each hydrated RSJS island emits a small vanilla-JS module plus seed state, served with a shared runtime around 1.3 KB gzipped.
Proxy one route to Proa, leave the rest on Next.js or Rails, then compare latency and cost in production.
call Proa over FFI from Node, Go, Python, Ruby, or Java.
